screens.title: Understanding UV Unwrapping
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will make UV unwrapping feel like a practical skill, not a mystery. UV unwrapping is the process of flattening a 3D mesh into a 2D map so a texture image can be placed exactly where you need it. You will learn why this matters for game development — from precise texture placement to baking and efficient atlasing — and how to choose between automatic methods like Smart UV Project and manual control with marked seams. We will also practice a short hands-on crate unwrap so you can see how seams, islands, and the 0‑1 UV space work together. As you follow along, focus on common pitfalls: stretching, overlapping islands, and unapplied transforms that break an otherwise clean unwrap. By the end of the chapter you will be able to decide when to rely on an automatic unwrap and when to mark seams for predictable, paintable UV islands. Consider the question you should ask before unwrapping: which parts of this model need pixel‑perfect control and which can be automatic?

screens.title: What is a UV map?
screens.narratorSegment: A UV map is the flattened 2D representation of a 3D mesh's surface. When you unwrap a model you assign each face a place in the UV space, which is measured along two axes: U and V. Think of U and V like X and Y for the texture image. This map tells Blender exactly which pixel on an image corresponds to which point on the mesh. The key consequence is control: with a proper UV map you can place a high‑resolution logo, bake normal maps from a detailed sculpt to a low‑poly mesh, or pack multiple parts of a character into a single texture atlas. A common misconception is that UVs automatically preserve area; they do not. A UV island must be scaled proportionally if you want consistent texel density. For example, the face of a crate should occupy UV space roughly proportional to its visible area in the game to avoid blurry details. Close by asking: does this UV layout give each important surface enough pixels? What is a UV map? means uv map = the 2d coordinates that map each mesh face to a specific point on a texture image.. In practical terms, a precise 2d layout that defines how textures wrap a 3d model. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

UV Map explained
How the 3D → 2D mapping controls where each texture pixel lands on your mesh.
• U and V are the axes of texture space, analogous to X and Y in 3D.
• Each UV island corresponds to a connected set of faces from the 3D model.
• UVs give you pixel‑level control for painting and baking workflows.
Example
A crate's face occupies a rectangular UV island so a logo can be placed on that face without distortion.

Treat UVs as the mapping plan between your texture pixels and mesh surface; adjust island scale for consistent texel density.

Visual: UV island cards
Island
A connected cluster of faces that will be textured together.
0‑1 space
The square texture region used by the engine; islands should fit within it.
Texel density
The pixel density per surface area; keep it consistent for visual quality.
Stretch
A mismatch between 3D area and UV area that causes distortion.

screens.title: Preparing a mesh and the UV Editor
screens.narratorSegment: A predictable unwrap starts with preparation. First, apply any scale and rotation you've performed in Object Mode — use Ctrl + A to apply Scale and Rotation. If you skip this step, Blender will unwrap using scaled coordinates and islands may stretch unexpectedly. Next, enter Edit Mode with Tab so you can select faces and edges. Change one window pane to the UV Editor; at first it may be empty or show a jumbled layout. The UV Editor is where you'll move, rotate and scale islands using G, R and S, much like operations in the 3D View. Remember to think in terms of the 0‑1 space: the UV square represents the texture image, so islands outside that square will not sample the main texture properly. A common misconception is that the UV Editor only shows geometry; it also provides overlays like Display Stretch to visualize distortion. Practice: apply transforms, select a face, and preview how the UV changes in the editor. This preparation prevents many common unwrap failures. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Preparing a mesh
Preparation steps
A reliable unwrap follows a short checklist to avoid distortion and surprises.
  1. Apply Scale and Rotation in Object Mode (Ctrl + A > Scale / Rotation).
  2. Enter Edit Mode (Tab) and switch a pane to UV Editor.
  3. Select faces or edges you plan to unwrap and preview in the UV Editor.
  4. Use Display Stretch to detect where seams or different methods are needed.
Common mistake

Not applying scale causes unpredictable island sizing and hidden stretching after unwrap.

Quick reference
Apply transforms: Ctrl + A > Scale / Rotation
Enter Edit Mode: Tab
Open UV Editor: change a window to "UV Editor"
Unwrap menu: U > choose method
Key Takeaway
Preparation reduces trial and error. Always fix transforms and preview UVs before committing to seams.

screens.title: Automatic Unwraps: Smart UV Project vs Projections
screens.narratorSegment: Blender offers several automatic unwrapping methods and each has a place in your toolkit. Smart UV Project analyzes a mesh and attempts to create non‑overlapping islands with minimal distortion. It's fast and useful for initial passes, but it often splits the surface into many small, scattered islands that are hard to paint manually. Projection methods like Cube, Cylinder, and Sphere project UVs from a geometric primitive — Cube Projection is great for boxy objects and will often give clean rectangular islands for faces aligned to axes. Cylinder Projection handles curved sides well but can badly distort circular caps. Follow Active Quads keeps quad topology aligned and is useful for long regular strips. A helpful contrast: use Smart UV Project when you need speed and non‑overlap; use Cube/Cylinder/Sphere when the object matches the primitive shape; use Mark Seam when you need precise control. An example is a barrel: Cylinder Projection works for sides but the top and bottom should be separated with seams to avoid cap stretching. Decide based on shape, need for painting, and whether you'll bake maps later. Automatic Unwraps: Smart UV Project vs Projections means automatic methods are quick but trade control; choose projection when geometry matches the primitive and mark seams for precision.. In practical terms, when to use smart uv project, cube projection, cylinder/sphere, or follow active quads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Automatic Unwraps
Method comparison
Smart UV Project
Fast automatic unwrap that minimizes overlap but can create many small islands that complicate manual painting.
Cube/Cylinder/Sphere Projection
Project from a geometric primitive; clean for matching shapes but needs seams for caps and poles.
Follow Active Quads / Lightmap Pack
Useful for quad grids and lightmap baking; each has tradeoffs in distortion and packing efficiency.
Scenario
You have a barrel. Cylinder Projection handles the sides but top and bottom caps will stretch if projected with the cylinder. Mark seams around the top and bottom and unwrap to separate cap islands for clean results.
Misconception

Automatic equals perfect. In reality, automatic unwrapping trades human intent for speed and often requires manual cleanup for painting and baking.

screens.title: Marking seams: the manual unwrap
screens.narratorSegment: Marking seams is the manual technique that gives you the cleanest, most paintable UV islands. The process imitates cutting a cardboard box: choose edges where the seam will be least visible, such as the underside of an arm or the back of a head, and mark them so Blender knows where to cut the mesh. In Edit Mode, switch to Edge Select, pick the edges, then use Ctrl + E and choose Mark Seam; marked edges appear red. After marking seams, select all faces and press U then Unwrap. Blender uses the seams to flatten the mesh into islands. A useful strategy is to place seams along natural material breaks or hidden areas, balancing fewer seams (to avoid visible lines) against enough cuts to prevent stretching. A common mistake is marking too many random seams which fragments islands and makes painting harder. Example: on a cube you mark the top and bottom loops and a single vertical seam to produce six well‑shaped rectangular islands for texturing. Marking seams: the manual unwrap means select edges in edge select mode, mark seam (ctrl + e), then unwrap (u > unwrap) to create predictable uv islands.. In practical terms, define cuts where a mesh should be separated to flatten into islands. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Marking seams
Step-by-step seam marking
Follow a few deliberate steps to produce clean, paintable islands.
  1. Enter Edit Mode and switch to Edge Select.
  2. Select edges along natural breaks or hidden areas.
  3. Press Ctrl + E > Mark Seam; edges turn red.
  4. Select all faces (A) and press U > Unwrap to flatten using those seams.
Analogy & example
Like cutting a cardboard box: choose cuts that hide joins and allow the surface to lie flat. For a cube: mark top and bottom loops and a vertical back seam to create six rectangular islands.
Key Takeaway
Seams are intentional cuts. Place them where paintability and minimal visible joins are balanced.

screens.title: Navigating and manipulating UV islands
screens.narratorSegment: Once islands exist in the UV Editor you must arrange them for texture painting, baking, or atlasing. The core transforms are the same as in the 3D View: G to move, R to rotate, and S to scale. Select all UVs and scale them to maximize coverage inside the 0‑1 square while keeping important islands proportionate to their visible area on the model. Use proportional scaling to maintain texel density across surfaces that share importance. When packing, avoid overlap unless you intentionally mirror details. The UV Editor also offers Display Stretch so you can see which areas will distort — blue means compression, red means stretching. A common error is leaving islands outside the 0‑1 square; those parts may sample a different texture or appear missing in an engine. Example workflow: after unwrapping a crate, scale each face island to fill the square evenly, rotate islands to align a grid texture, and pack them to maximize the atlas. Finish by checking with the stretch overlay and adjusting seams if needed. Editor controls and workflow
Move, rotate, scale and pack islands to make the most of the 0‑1 texture area.
Move: G
Rotate: R
Scale: S
Select all: A
Pack: use manual arrangement to maximize space
Check stretch: View > Display Stretch

screens.title: Common UV issues and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: Common problems are predictable and each has a clear fix. Stretching or distortion happens when the UV area does not match the 3D surface area; visualize it with Display Stretch and adjust seams or use a different unwrap method to redistribute UV area. Overlapping UVs make two surfaces share the same texture pixels; this is sometimes intentional for mirrored parts but usually wrong for unique textures. Fix overlap by moving or scaling islands and ensuring unique placement inside 0‑1 space. Too many seams fragment islands and make painting more difficult; reduce seams along visible areas, placing them where joins are less noticeable. Finally, unapplied scale or rotation in Object Mode causes inconsistent island sizes after unwrapping; always apply transforms first. Example: if a barrel's cap is red in the stretch overlay, separate it with seams and unwrap again. These fixes let you move from a messy automatic unwrap to a clean, artist‑friendly layout. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Common issues
Problem → Diagnosis → Fix
Stretching
Diagnose with Display Stretch; fix by adding seams or redistributing UV area to match surface area.
Overlapping UVs
Diagnose by selecting islands and checking for stacked outlines; fix by moving or repacking islands or intentionally mirror only where suitable.
Too many seams

screens.title: Texture atlases and efficient UV packing
screens.narratorSegment: Texture atlases combine multiple textures into a single image to improve performance and reduce draw calls in game engines. Well‑unwrapped UVs allow you to place different parts of a model or different models onto specific regions of an atlas. The goal is to use the 0‑1 UV square efficiently so important surfaces get more pixels and empty gaps are minimized. When packing, make islands proportional to their visual importance — a player's face should occupy more UV area than a shoe sole that’s rarely seen up close. Avoid overlapping unless you intentionally mirror parts to reuse pixels. Lightmap Pack is a Blender option aimed at baking, providing tight packing but sometimes with high distortion; choose carefully if you need low distortion for painting. A practical step: measure visible area, scale islands to balance texel density, then manually nudge islands to fill remaining space. Ask yourself: does this atlas allocation reflect how the model will be seen in the game? screens.title: Baking and UVs: why clean topology helps
screens.narratorSegment: Baking transfers surface detail from a high‑poly mesh to a low‑poly one and depends entirely on UVs. If UVs overlap or stretch, baked maps like normal or ambient occlusion will be incorrect or produce seams. Clean, non‑overlapping UVs and consistent texel density ensure baked information aligns with the low‑poly surface. Before baking, verify that seams are placed where normal discontinuities are acceptable and that islands do not intersect. A subtle but important point is that baking tools sample texels based on UV coordinates; that means improperly packed islands or islands outside 0‑1 can result in missing or misaligned bake data. Example: when baking a high‑poly sculpt to a game mesh, use a single island per logical area where possible and avoid overlapping unless intentional for mirrored details. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will make UV unwrapping feel like a practical skill, not a mystery. UV unwrapping is the process of flattening a 3D mesh into a 2D map so a texture image can be placed exactly where you need it. You will learn why this matters for game development — from precise texture placement to baking and efficient atlasing — and how to choose between automatic methods like Smart UV Project and manual control with marked seams. We will also practice a short hands-on crate unwrap so you can see how seams, islands, and the 0‑1 UV space work together. As you follow along, focus on common pitfalls: stretching, overlapping islands, and unapplied transforms that break an otherwise clean unwrap. By the end of the chapter you will be able to decide when to rely on an automatic unwrap and when to mark seams for predictable, paintable UV islands. Consider the question you should ask before unwrapping: which parts of this model need pixel‑perfect control and which can be automatic?

Over the next screens you'll build a practical skill set for UV unwrapping. First, we define UV unwrapping and why it is essential for game textures, so you can justify decisions about seams and atlases. Second, you'll learn to read and edit UV maps in the UV Editor, moving, scaling and rotating islands to fit the 0‑1 space and preserve texel density. Third, we'll practice the three basic methods Blender provides—Smart UV Project, geometric projections like Cube Projection, and manual seam marking—so you can pick the right tool for each model. Fourth, you'll diagnose and fix common issues such as stretching and overlapping, and learn the safety steps like applying scale and rotation before an unwrap. Each objective links a clear ability to a reason it matters in pipelines: baking, painting, and game performance. Imagine needing to paint a chest logo: you will know whether to mark seams for a large chest island or accept an automatic unwrap for less important parts. These are the milestones that make an unwrapped model production‑ready.

These objectives tie directly into the hands‑on lab you'll follow. First, you should be able to prepare a mesh by applying scale and rotation so unwrapping behaves predictably. Second, mark seams strategically to create contiguous islands for text painting, choosing seam placement where they are least visible. Third, use the UV Editor to pack islands into the 0‑1 space with consistent texel density, so details like logos retain resolution. Fourth, evaluate results with the stretch overlay and remove overlapping islands unless mirroring is intentional. Each milestone helps you move from a rough automatic unwrap to a model that can be baked, painted, and exported to a game engine. In practice, that means on the crate exercise you will mark seams, unwrap, arrange six rectangular islands and test a grid texture to confirm there is no stretching. Keep the question in mind: does this island need unique texture pixels, or can it share space with another mirrored island?

A UV map is the flattened 2D representation of a 3D mesh's surface. When you unwrap a model you assign each face a place in the UV space, which is measured along two axes: U and V. Think of U and V like X and Y for the texture image. This map tells Blender exactly which pixel on an image corresponds to which point on the mesh. The key consequence is control: with a proper UV map you can place a high‑resolution logo, bake normal maps from a detailed sculpt to a low‑poly mesh, or pack multiple parts of a character into a single texture atlas. A common misconception is that UVs automatically preserve area; they do not. A UV island must be scaled proportionally if you want consistent texel density. For example, the face of a crate should occupy UV space roughly proportional to its visible area in the game to avoid blurry details. Close by asking: does this UV layout give each important surface enough pixels? What is a UV map? means uv map = the 2d coordinates that map each mesh face to a specific point on a texture image.. In practical terms, a precise 2d layout that defines how textures wrap a 3d model. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A predictable unwrap starts with preparation. First, apply any scale and rotation you've performed in Object Mode — use Ctrl + A to apply Scale and Rotation. If you skip this step, Blender will unwrap using scaled coordinates and islands may stretch unexpectedly. Next, enter Edit Mode with Tab so you can select faces and edges. Change one window pane to the UV Editor; at first it may be empty or show a jumbled layout. The UV Editor is where you'll move, rotate and scale islands using G, R and S, much like operations in the 3D View. Remember to think in terms of the 0‑1 space: the UV square represents the texture image, so islands outside that square will not sample the main texture properly. A common misconception is that the UV Editor only shows geometry; it also provides overlays like Display Stretch to visualize distortion. Practice: apply transforms, select a face, and preview how the UV changes in the editor. This preparation prevents many common unwrap failures. Preparing a mesh and the UV Editor means always apply scale/rotation, enter edit mode, and open the uv editor to reliably control unwrapping and avoid unexpected distortion.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Blender offers several automatic unwrapping methods and each has a place in your toolkit. Smart UV Project analyzes a mesh and attempts to create non‑overlapping islands with minimal distortion. It's fast and useful for initial passes, but it often splits the surface into many small, scattered islands that are hard to paint manually. Projection methods like Cube, Cylinder, and Sphere project UVs from a geometric primitive — Cube Projection is great for boxy objects and will often give clean rectangular islands for faces aligned to axes. Cylinder Projection handles curved sides well but can badly distort circular caps. Follow Active Quads keeps quad topology aligned and is useful for long regular strips. A helpful contrast: use Smart UV Project when you need speed and non‑overlap; use Cube/Cylinder/Sphere when the object matches the primitive shape; use Mark Seam when you need precise control. An example is a barrel: Cylinder Projection works for sides but the top and bottom should be separated with seams to avoid cap stretching. Decide based on shape, need for painting, and whether you'll bake maps later. Automatic Unwraps: Smart UV Project vs Projections means automatic methods are quick but trade control; choose projection when geometry matches the primitive and mark seams for precision.. In practical terms, when to use smart uv project, cube projection, cylinder/sphere, or follow active quads. Marking seams is the manual technique that gives you the cleanest, most paintable UV islands. The process imitates cutting a cardboard box: choose edges where the seam will be least visible, such as the underside of an arm or the back of a head, and mark them so Blender knows where to cut the mesh. In Edit Mode, switch to Edge Select, pick the edges, then use Ctrl + E and choose Mark Seam; marked edges appear red. After marking seams, select all faces and press U then Unwrap. Blender uses the seams to flatten the mesh into islands. A useful strategy is to place seams along natural material breaks or hidden areas, balancing fewer seams (to avoid visible lines) against enough cuts to prevent stretching. A common mistake is marking too many random seams which fragments islands and makes painting harder. Example: on a cube you mark the top and bottom loops and a single vertical seam to produce six well‑shaped rectangular islands for texturing. Once islands exist in the UV Editor you must arrange them for texture painting, baking, or atlasing. The core transforms are the same as in the 3D View: G to move, R to rotate, and S to scale. Select all UVs and scale them to maximize coverage inside the 0‑1 square while keeping important islands proportionate to their visible area on the model. Use proportional scaling to maintain texel density across surfaces that share importance. When packing, avoid overlap unless you intentionally mirror details. The UV Editor also offers Display Stretch so you can see which areas will distort — blue means compression, red means stretching. A common error is leaving islands outside the 0‑1 square; those parts may sample a different texture or appear missing in an engine. Example workflow: after unwrapping a crate, scale each face island to fill the square evenly, rotate islands to align a grid texture, and pack them to maximize the atlas. Finish by checking with the stretch overlay and adjusting seams if needed. Common problems are predictable and each has a clear fix. Stretching or distortion happens when the UV area does not match the 3D surface area; visualize it with Display Stretch and adjust seams or use a different unwrap method to redistribute UV area. Overlapping UVs make two surfaces share the same texture pixels; this is sometimes intentional for mirrored parts but usually wrong for unique textures. Fix overlap by moving or scaling islands and ensuring unique placement inside 0‑1 space. Too many seams fragment islands and make painting more difficult; reduce seams along visible areas, placing them where joins are less noticeable. Finally, unapplied scale or rotation in Object Mode causes inconsistent island sizes after unwrapping; always apply transforms first. Example: if a barrel's cap is red in the stretch overlay, separate it with seams and unwrap again. These fixes let you move from a messy automatic unwrap to a clean, artist‑friendly layout.
